1.1.stem: A caller claiming to be from the school IT office says a student's account will be deleted today unless they read back the code just texted to their phone. Which TWO levers are combined here?
1.1.why: Claiming to be IT is authority; 'deleted today' is urgency.

1.1.stem: Why would an attacker ask a victim to read back a code that was just texted to them?
opts: The code is a one-time password that lets the attacker finish logging in as the victim
The code repairs the victim's phone
The code proves the attacker is from IT
1.1.why: Relaying an OTP lets the attacker pass the second factor.

1.1.stem: Which email detail is the MOST reliable phishing indicator?
opts: The sender's domain is a look-alike of the real organization's domain
The email has a colorful logo
The email was sent on a weekday
1.1.why: Look-alike domains are hard evidence; logos and greetings are easily copied.

1.1.stem: A student gets a suspicious message that appears to come from a teacher's real school address. What should they do FIRST?
opts: Confirm with the teacher through a separate channel before acting
Click the link to see where it goes
Reply asking if it is real
1.1.why: Real accounts can be compromised; verify out-of-band.

1.1.stem: A text says: 'You won a gift card! Only 3 left. Claim in the next 5 minutes.' Which levers are present?
1.1.why: 'Only 3 left' is scarcity; '5 minutes' is urgency.

1.1.stem: Which target is MOST likely to be chosen for an elicitation attack aimed at learning a company's internal systems?
opts: A new help-desk employee active on public social media
A random person at a bus stop
A retired employee from 20 years ago
1.1.why: New, public-facing staff with current knowledge and a social footprint are attractive targets.

1.1.stem: Which combination BEST reduces phishing risk in a school?
opts: Email filtering, staff and student training, and MFA on accounts
1.1.why: Layering technical filtering, awareness and MFA limits both delivery and impact.

1.1.stem: A user notices their email now auto-forwards to an unknown external address. What does this MOST likely indicate?
opts: The account was compromised and a forwarding rule was added
The spam filter is too strict
1.1.why: Unexpected forwarding rules are a common indicator of a taken-over mailbox.

1.1.stem: An attacker sends dozens of harmless, friendly messages to a staff member over two weeks before asking for a 'quick favor' involving the staff portal. What is the purpose of the earlier messages?
opts: Building trust and familiarity so the later request seems normal
Filling the inbox to cause a denial of service
1.1.why: Rapport lowers suspicion before the real request.

1.1.stem: Why is reporting a phishing email to IT better than just deleting it?
opts: IT can block the sender and warn others who received the same message
Reporting makes the email disappear for the sender
Reporting changes the user's password automatically
1.1.why: A report lets defenders protect everyone, not just one inbox.

1.1.stem: An online quiz asks for your first pet's name, your street growing up, and your mother's maiden name. These are commonly used as:
1.1.why: Quizzes like this elicit answers to security questions.

1.1.stem: Which observation is an indicator of compromise rather than just a suspicious message?
opts: Friends report receiving messages from your account that you didn't send
You received an email with a typo
An email arrives from an unknown sender
A newsletter has a bright banner
1.1.why: Messages sent from your account without you show it is being used by someone else.

1.1.stem: After clicking a phishing link and entering a password, what should a user do FIRST?
opts: Change that password from a trusted device and report the incident
Wait to see if anything happens
Delete the email and say nothing
1.1.why: Rotating the stolen secret quickly and reporting limits the damage.

1.1.stem: A phishing campaign targets a district's payroll staff right before payday with fake 'update your direct deposit' forms. Why is the impact HIGH?
opts: Successful victims can have paychecks redirected to attacker accounts
1.1.why: Financial redirection causes direct monetary loss.

1.1.stem: Why do phishing emails often hide the real link behind button text like 'Verify now'?
opts: So the victim doesn't see the true, suspicious destination
Buttons load faster than text links
1.1.why: Disguised links conceal the attacker's domain.

1.1.stem: Which is a technical control against phishing?
opts: An email filter that flags messages from look-alike domains
A poster about phishing in the hallway
1.1.why: Filtering software is a technical control; posters, policies and training are not.

1.1.stem: A security team wants to measure whether training is working. Which method gives the MOST direct evidence?
opts: Run an authorized simulated phishing exercise and track report and click rates
Count how many posters are on the walls
Ask students if they liked the training

1.2.stem: An attacker uses software to try thousands of common passwords against a website login. This is:
1.2.why: Automated guessing is a password attack.

opts: A long random passphrase of unrelated words unique to this site
1.2.why: Length, randomness and uniqueness beat short complex-looking patterns.

1.2.stem: A user gets an unexpected 'Approve sign-in?' push notification on their phone while not logging in. What does this MOST likely mean?
opts: Someone already has their password and is trying to pass MFA
1.2.why: An MFA prompt you didn't trigger means the first factor is already compromised.

1.2.stem: In the situation where a user receives an MFA prompt they did not trigger, what should they do?
opts: Deny the prompt, change the password, and report it
Approve it to make it stop
Ignore it and keep using the account
1.2.why: Denying blocks the attacker; changing the password removes the stolen factor.

1.2.stem: An attacker repeatedly sends MFA push prompts at 2 a.m. hoping the victim taps Approve to stop them. Why can this work?
opts: Tired, annoyed users may approve just to end the notifications
Push prompts approve themselves after ten tries
The phone automatically trusts repeated prompts
1.2.why: Prompt fatigue exploits human behavior, not a technical flaw.

1.2.stem: Which MFA method is MOST resistant to the repeated-prompt attack above?
opts: A hardware security key or number-matching prompt that requires active input
1.2.why: Methods requiring physical presence or matching a number defeat blind approvals.

1.2.stem: A student reuses one password for school email, gaming, and a shopping site. The gaming site is breached. Which accounts are at risk?
1.2.why: Reused credentials can be tried everywhere.

1.2.stem: Which address bar shows the REAL school portal login?
1.2.why: Only the first is on the school's own registered domain.

1.2.stem: What does 'sign out of all sessions' accomplish after a password reset?
opts: It ends any logins an attacker may already have open
1.2.why: Existing sessions can survive a password change unless ended.

1.2.stem: Which is an example of 'something you have' in MFA?
opts: A code from an authenticator app on your phone
1.2.why: The phone with the app is a possession factor.

1.2.stem: An attacker has a user's password but not their phone. Which control stops the login?
1.2.why: Without the second factor, the password alone fails.

1.2.stem: What is the PURPOSE of a 'new sign-in' alert email?
opts: To let the user detect logins they didn't make
1.2.why: Alerts are a detective control for account misuse.

1.2.stem: Why do attackers build fake login pages instead of guessing passwords?
opts: Victims type their real password straight into the attacker's page
Guessing is illegal but fake pages are not
1.2.why: Credential harvesting gets the exact password with one victim mistake.

1.2.stem: A password manager auto-fills credentials only on the exact saved domain. How does this help against fake login pages?
opts: It won't fill the password on a look-alike domain, warning the user
1.2.why: Domain matching makes look-alike pages stand out.

1.2.stem: A review finds several staff accounts with no MFA and reused passwords. How should this be recorded?
opts: A vulnerability increasing the likelihood of account takeover
An accepted risk with no action
1.2.why: Missing MFA plus reuse is a documented weakness to fix.

1.2.stem: Account activity shows a login from Seattle at 9:00 and from Singapore at 9:05 for the same user. What does this suggest?
opts: Impossible travel: the credentials are being used by someone else
1.2.why: Physical travel that fast is impossible, so another party is using the account.

1.2.stem: Which account should have MFA turned on FIRST?
opts: The primary email account that receives password resets
A forum account with no personal data
1.2.why: Protecting the reset channel protects every account linked to it.

1.3.stem: Which public Wi-Fi network is MOST suspicious?
opts: An open network named 'Free_Airport_WiFi_FAST' not listed on airport signs
The network name printed on the café's menu
A network a staff member confirms
1.3.why: Unverified, too-good names on open networks are classic evil twin bait.

1.3.stem: Which device setting MOST reduces risk on public Wi-Fi?
opts: Turn on the device's firewall and turn off file sharing
1.3.why: A host firewall and disabled sharing cut exposure to others on the network.

1.3.stem: Why do evil twins often use stronger signal strength than the real network?
opts: Devices tend to connect to the strongest signal with a known name
1.3.why: Auto-join prefers the strongest matching SSID.

1.3.stem: A traveler must check a bank account in an airport. Which option is SAFEST?
opts: Use the phone's cellular data instead of public Wi-Fi
Use the network with the most bars
1.3.why: Cellular data avoids the shared, untrusted local network.

1.3.stem: Which activity on unencrypted public Wi-Fi has the HIGHEST impact if intercepted?
opts: Logging into a site that doesn't use HTTPS
1.3.why: Credentials sent without encryption can be captured and reused.

1.3.stem: Which attack targets the AVAILABILITY of a wireless network?
1.3.why: Jamming prevents use of the network: availability.

1.3.stem: Which pair of protections BEST covers both eavesdropping and fake login pages on public Wi-Fi?
opts: VPN plus checking the domain before entering credentials
1.3.why: A VPN protects traffic; domain checks catch credential harvesting the VPN won't stop.

1.3.stem: While on hotel Wi-Fi, a browser warns that a familiar site's security certificate is invalid. What is the BEST interpretation?
opts: The connection may be intercepted; do not proceed
The site is having a sale
The Wi-Fi is faster than usual
1.3.why: Certificate warnings on known sites can signal an on-path attacker.

1.3.stem: An attacker parks near a coffee shop with an antenna, captures traffic, and later cracks a weak Wi-Fi password offline. Which earlier activity helped them find the shop?
1.3.why: War driving maps networks and their security from a vehicle.

opts: Traffic between your device and the VPN server
Files stored on your hard drive
1.3.why: A VPN protects data in transit through its tunnel.

1.3.stem: A VPN is connected, but the user types a password into a phishing site. Does the VPN prevent the theft?
opts: No, the VPN encrypts the path but the user still sends the password to the attacker
Yes, the password is encrypted forever
No, because VPNs only work at home
1.3.why: VPNs protect transport, not bad destinations.

1.3.stem: Which tool helps a network owner detect jamming?
opts: Monitoring for unusual radio noise and sudden connection loss
1.3.why: Jamming shows up as interference and widespread disconnection.

opts: The broadcast name of a wireless network

1.3.stem: Why should laptops 'forget' public networks after use?
opts: So they don't auto-connect later to an evil twin with the same name

1.3.stem: A hospital's guest Wi-Fi is open and shares a network with medical devices. Which risk is MOST severe?
opts: Guests could reach or disrupt medical devices
Guests could see the lobby TV
Guests could use too much bandwidth for videos
Guests could change their own wallpapers
1.3.why: Access to critical devices threatens safety and availability.

1.3.stem: An access-point scan shows two networks with the same SSID, one from the café's router brand and one from an unknown laptop. What should staff conclude?
opts: A possible evil twin is operating
It's a guest network for staff
1.3.why: A duplicate SSID from unknown hardware suggests a rogue AP.

1.3.stem: After the evil twin above is found, which action should staff take and log?
opts: Report it, warn customers to use the posted SSID, and remove or block the rogue device
1.3.why: Removing the threat and informing users is the correct response.

1.4.stem: An AI tool writes 10,000 unique phishing emails in different languages in minutes. Which aspect of the attack does AI MOST change?
1.4.why: AI lowers cost per message and raises fluency.

1.4.stem: A family agrees on a secret word to confirm emergencies on the phone. What is this control defending against?
1.4.why: A pre-shared safe word verifies identity regardless of how real a voice sounds.

1.4.stem: How can an attacker clone a person's voice?
opts: Train AI on a short sample of public audio such as videos or voicemails
1.4.why: Voice models need only seconds of recorded speech.

1.4.stem: A video call with a 'manager' has slightly delayed lip movement, and the manager refuses to turn their head when asked. What should the employee suspect?
1.4.why: Artifacts plus refusing simple liveness checks are deepfake warning signs, though procedure matters more.

1.4.stem: Which policy BEST protects a company against deepfake-driven requests regardless of detection quality?
opts: Any payment or credential request must be verified through a known, separate channel
1.4.why: Out-of-band verification doesn't depend on spotting the fake.

1.4.stem: Which person is at HIGHEST risk of voice-clone impersonation?
opts: A school principal who records daily announcements posted online
A person with no online presence
A person who never speaks on the phone
1.4.why: Abundant public audio makes cloning easier.

1.4.stem: An LLM is tricked by hidden text on a web page into revealing data or following attacker instructions. This is called:
1.4.why: Malicious instructions smuggled into an AI's input is prompt injection.

1.4.stem: Why is it risky to let an AI assistant read your email AND send money automatically?
opts: A malicious email could instruct the AI to take harmful actions
Emails are always safe for AI
1.4.why: Untrusted input plus powerful actions enables prompt-injection abuse.

1.4.stem: An attacker uses AI to collect a target's public posts, job history, and friends, then writes a tailored message. Which attack phase is AI accelerating?
Which signal can still help detect AI-written phishing even when grammar is perfect?
opts: The sender domain, the request, and the pressure to act fast
1.4.why: Context and intent remain detectable; language quality is no longer a tell.

1.4.stem: Which is the BEST response to an urgent voice message from a 'relative' asking for gift cards?
opts: Hang up and call the relative back on their known number

1.4.stem: An analyst notes that executives' voices are widely available online and payment approvals are done by phone. How should this be documented?
opts: A risk of deepfake voice fraud due to phone-only payment approval
1.4.why: A vulnerable process combined with available audio is a documented risk.

1.4.stem: AI tools that automatically generate many slight variations of malware are MOST intended to evade:
1.4.why: Each variant has a new signature that defenders haven't seen.

1.4.stem: To counter AI-generated malware variants, defenders should add:
1.4.why: Behavior detection catches new variants that act the same.

1.4.stem: Why does AI increase the LIKELIHOOD of successful phishing across a population?
opts: More convincing messages reach more people at very low cost
1.4.why: Better quality times greater volume raises success odds.

1.4.stem: A 'vendor' emails a new bank account for invoices; the writing perfectly matches the real vendor's style. The vendor's domain differs by one letter. What is the decisive evidence?
1.4.why: AI can copy style, but the domain reveals the impersonation.

1.4.stem: After nearly falling for a deepfake call, a business adds a rule: changes to payment details require a call-back and second approver. This is best described as:
opts: Implementing a managerial mitigation and documenting it
1.4.why: A new procedure is a managerial control put in place to reduce risk.

1.5.stem: Which task is AI MOST useful for in a security operations center?
opts: Summarizing and prioritizing large volumes of alerts
1.5.why: Triage at scale is AI's strongest defensive use.

1.5.stem: An AI detector misses a real intrusion because the attacker behaved like a normal user. This is a:
1.5.why: A missed real attack is a false negative.

1.5.stem: Why must anomaly detection models first learn a baseline?
opts: They need to know what normal looks like to flag deviations
1.5.why: Anomalies are defined relative to normal behavior.

1.5.stem: An AI assistant suggests a firewall rule. What should the analyst do before applying it?
opts: Review and test it to confirm it does what's intended
Apply it immediately to save time
1.5.why: Human review catches incorrect or harmful AI suggestions.

1.5.stem: An AI model flags 30% of normal logins as suspicious. Which change BEST reduces alert fatigue without ignoring real threats?
opts: Tune thresholds and retrain on better data, then measure false negatives too
1.5.why: Tuning must balance false positives against missed attacks.

1.5.stem: An attacker feeds misleading data into the logs an AI system learns from, so attacks look normal. This is:
An email filter that uses machine learning to score how likely a message is to be phishing is an example of:
1.5.why: ML scoring of messages is automated detection.

1.5.stem: Which policy BEST governs staff use of public AI chatbots at work?
opts: Allow approved tools only and forbid pasting confidential data
Allow any tool with any data
Require chatbots to write all reports
1.5.why: Approval plus data rules manage leakage risk.

1.5.stem: An AI summary says 'no malicious activity' but the raw log shows a login from a blocked country. Which should the analyst trust?
What is a key benefit of AI ranking alerts by severity?
opts: Analysts spend limited time on the most dangerous events first
1.5.why: Prioritization improves response to high-risk events.

1.5.stem: A team automates blocking of IPs flagged by AI. Which safeguard is MOST important?
opts: Human review for high-impact blocks plus an easy rollback
Disabling the AI after one week
1.5.why: Automation errors can cut off legitimate users; review and rollback limit harm.

1.5.stem: Which risk is MOST associated with relying fully on AI for security decisions?
opts: Confident but wrong outputs going unchecked
1.5.why: Unverified AI mistakes can cause missed attacks or wrong actions.

1.5.stem: Which combination gives the BEST detection coverage?
opts: AI anomaly detection plus signature rules plus human analysts
1.5.why: Layered detection covers each method's blind spots.

1.5.stem: An LLM helps draft an incident report. What must the analyst verify before submitting it?
opts: Every timeline fact matches the logs
The report is under one page
1.5.why: Reports must be accurate to the evidence.

1.5.stem: What does 'human in the loop' mean for AI security tools?
opts: A person reviews and approves important AI decisions

1.5.stem: An AI tool flags a student account downloading 500 files at 3 a.m. from a new device. Which analyst step comes FIRST?
opts: Verify with logs and the account owner whether the activity is legitimate
Ignore it because AI is often wrong
1.5.why: Confirm the alert with evidence before acting.

1.5.stem: Why might attackers test their malware against public AI-based scanners before launching it?
opts: To adjust it until it is no longer detected
